desc:
For a positive integer x, let s(x) be the sum of the squares of its decimal digits. For example s(47) = 42 + 72 = 65 and s(100) = 1.

Given n, count the integers x with 1 ≤ x ≤ n for which s(x) is a perfect square (1, 4, 9, 16, and so on).

n = 10  -> 10   (s(x) = 1 to 81 for x = 1 to 9, and s(10) = 1)
n = 20  -> 11   (the numbers 1 to 10, plus 20 with s(20) = 4)
hints: Checking every x from 1 to n is too slow when n is near two billion. Think about how the numbers below n are built: a shared prefix of n, then a smaller digit, then any digits.
For a fixed number of free trailing digits, count how many of them give each digit-square-sum once and reuse that table. The sums never exceed 81 for each digit, so the table is small.

Walk the digits of n from left to right. At each position, for every smaller digit, add the count of suffixes whose total makes the prefix sum plus that suffix sum a perfect square. Finally test n itself. Zero is not counted.
editorial: This is a digit DP. Pad every number below n to the length L of n with leading zeros; zeros add nothing to the square sum, so this changes nothing. A number that is below n has a longest common prefix with n, then a strictly smaller digit, then arbitrary digits.

Let ways[t][s] be the number of digit strings of length t whose squared digits sum to s. It satisfies ways[t][s] = sum over d of ways[t-1][s - d<sup>2</sup>], and s never exceeds 81t. For each position i and each digit d smaller than the digit of n there, the block of numbers with that prefix has suffix length t = L - i - 1 and prefix sum p + d<sup>2</sup>. Add ways[t][s] for every s with p + d<sup>2</sup> + s a perfect square and at least 1.

Finally add n itself when its own digit-square-sum is a perfect square. The total work is about L * 10 * 81L operations, which is tiny. The value 0, whose sum is 0, is excluded by the requirement that the sum be at least 1.
time: O(L * 10 * 81L) for L digits of n
